frictionVectors.title: European gas diversification
frictionVectors.details: European efforts to reduce dependence on Algerian pipeline gas constrain Algiers' long-term bargaining power, despite continued demand for its exports.

frictionVectors.title: Regional security pressure
frictionVectors.details: Instability across the Sahel and strained relations with Morocco raise border-security costs and complicate infrastructure and trade planning.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito corridor geopolitics
frictionVectors.details: US and European backing for the corridor increases Angola's strategic value but also subjects transport and mineral infrastructure to major-power competition.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese debt and construction exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed infrastructure remains important, while debt-servicing obligations and oil-price volatility limit Luanda's policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Niger pipeline dispute
frictionVectors.details: Political tensions with Niger have threatened the operation and commercial viability of the oil-export pipeline linking Nigerien crude to Benin's coast.

frictionVectors.title: Cotonou infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Benin's logistics ambitions rely on foreign-financed port, road, and energy projects, creating exposure to external lenders and regional political shocks.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers partnership renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana's push for greater diamond marketing and revenue control strengthens sovereignty but risks prolonged friction with De Beers and its parent company.

frictionVectors.title: New-minerals investment terms
frictionVectors.details: Efforts to attract investment into copper, nickel, and other minerals must balance foreign capital needs against local processing and ownership demands.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security alignment
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou's closer security relationship with Russia reduces reliance on Western partners but creates new dependency risks and uncertainty around strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector control and smuggling
frictionVectors.details: State efforts to increase control over industrial and artisanal gold are challenged by insurgent taxation, informal networks, and weak enforcement outside major urban centers.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Governance
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater control over nickel, rare-earth and gold projects, but limited capital and technical capacity leave room for foreign investors to shape contracts and export chains.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Security Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Tensions with Rwanda and instability in eastern DRC constrain trade and security autonomy, while Burundi remains dependent on external partners for budgetary and development financing.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, airport and digital infrastructure rely heavily on European, Chinese and multilateral financing, creating long-term exposure to external creditors and strategic investors.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Security Burden
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's strategic Atlantic position brings opportunities in shipping and data connectivity but also requires outside assistance to police fisheries, trafficking routes and its extensive maritime zone.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Resource Chains
frictionVectors.details: Oil, gas, timber and mining projects remain dependent on multinational capital and opaque intermediaries, limiting domestic value capture and fiscal transparency.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and Sahel Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest, alongside insecurity near the Lake Chad basin, diverts state capacity and threatens transport corridors linking ports to inland markets.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Mining-Security Nexus
frictionVectors.details: Russian security personnel and affiliated commercial networks retain major influence around gold and diamond areas, exchanging protection and political backing for privileged resource access.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor and Border Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country remains reliant on neighboring states and external actors for trade routes, fuel and security, while armed groups continue to contest mineral-producing and transport zones.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Revenue Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon income remains central to state finance, but foreign operators, opaque revenue management and weak domestic refining capacity constrain sovereign control over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's strategic position between Libya, Sudan and the Central African Republic sustains reliance on foreign military, financial and diplomatic partners, limiting autonomy during political transition.

frictionVectors.title: French Control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France's administration of Mayotte remains the central sovereignty dispute, limiting Comoros' control over surrounding waters and migration policy. Moroni continues to rely on diplomatic pressure rather than coercive tools.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence for Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Weak domestic fiscal capacity leaves transport, energy, and telecommunications projects dependent on foreign aid and investors. This expands external leverage while offshore resource potential remains largely undeveloped.

frictionVectors.title: M23 Conflict and Regional Intervention
frictionVectors.details: Armed conflict in the east continues to erode Kinshasa's territorial control and expose mineral corridors to regional and transnational networks. Rwanda, neighboring states, and international security actors remain deeply implicated in the security environment.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Mining Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and Western firms compete for copper, cobalt, lithium, and other strategic minerals, while the state struggles to enforce contracts, taxation, and local processing. Renegotiation efforts have improved leverage but have not fundamentally displaced extractive dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Public finances and foreign-exchange earnings remain heavily tied to oil exports, leaving sovereignty vulnerable to price cycles and the terms set by international operators. Diversification and domestic value addition remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed infrastructure has expanded roads, ports, and public facilities but also reinforces creditor and contractor influence. Debt servicing and project transparency constrain the government's room to pursue fully autonomous development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capture of Cocoa Value
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire has strengthened regulation and domestic processing ambitions, but farmers and the state remain exposed to multinational trading, financing, and pricing structures. The country retains limited control over final-value distribution.

frictionVectors.title: External Security and Investment Dependence
frictionVectors.details: French, Gulf, Chinese, and other foreign capital remains important to ports, energy, and transport infrastructure. Rising insecurity in the northern Sahel also increases reliance on external intelligence, equipment, and security partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Competition
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its position through U.S., French, Chinese, Japanese, and other military facilities, but the concentration of external forces creates diplomatic exposure and limits strategic autonomy. Rivalry around the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden raises the stakes.

frictionVectors.title: Port Assets and Chinese Financing
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed ports, rail, and logistics projects have expanded Djibouti's connectivity while increasing debt and creditor leverage. Competition with Gulf-linked operators and neighboring Ethiopian trade interests further complicates control of the infrastructure network.

highlights: Gulf and IMF capital deepen dependence

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile security
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose Ethiopian dam operations it views as threatening downstream water security. Diplomatic engagement remains active but has not resolved binding rules for drought periods.

frictionVectors.title: External control of strategic assets
frictionVectors.details: Debt servicing and foreign-exchange pressures increase reliance on Gulf financing, IMF support, and asset sales. This can constrain Cairo's autonomy over ports, logistics, and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon decline
frictionVectors.details: Falling production and limited diversification threaten fiscal stability and bargaining power with international energy firms. LNG and offshore projects remain vulnerable to capital and technology dependence.

frictionVectors.title: External energy partnerships
frictionVectors.details: The government retains formal control over hydrocarbons but depends on foreign operators, markets, and financing. Opaque contracts and weak oversight limit broad domestic gains from resource extraction.

highlights: Red Sea position attracts strategic attention

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector dependency
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal production provides hard currency but relies heavily on foreign capital, technical expertise, and export channels. Limited transparency increases exposure to sanctions and reputational pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline has growing strategic value as regional powers compete over Red Sea access. External security interest can bring infrastructure opportunities while increasing pressure on Asmara's autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Economic reliance on South Africa
frictionVectors.details: Trade, transport, energy, and financial links with South Africa give Pretoria and regional markets substantial structural influence. Any disruption in South African logistics or customs access would quickly affect Eswatini.

frictionVectors.title: Export-sector vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Sugar and apparel industries depend on preferential market access, foreign investors, and external infrastructure. Shifts in trade rules or labor-compliance requirements could weaken sovereign policy space.

frictionVectors.title: Nile basin confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam expands Ethiopia's electricity and water-management leverage but remains a central security dispute with Egypt and Sudan. Absent a durable operating agreement, drought conditions could trigger renewed escalation.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and foreign-exchange shortages constrain infrastructure choices, while reliance on neighboring ports exposes Ethiopia to regional bargaining. Gulf, Chinese, and Western financing each offer leverage but also impose competing strategic expectations.

highlights: Junta-led transition seeks tighter control of oil and minerals
Manganese and railway infrastructure remain externally dependent

frictionVectors.title: Mining and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Gabon is seeking greater domestic value capture from manganese and other minerals, but Chinese and other foreign firms remain important for extraction, logistics, and financing.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector governance
frictionVectors.details: The transition government is asserting control over hydrocarbons and public assets while facing fiscal pressure and the need to maintain investor confidence.

highlights: Senegal remains the critical security and trade partner
Fisheries and port access expose sovereignty vulnerabilities

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing pressure
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing by foreign-linked fleets continues to strain coastal resources, enforcement capacity, and local food security.

frictionVectors.title: Senegal-linked infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for regional connectivity, security cooperation, and access routes, limiting strategic autonomy while providing essential stability.

highlights: Gold remains the strongest national resource anchor
Debt stress constrains control over infrastructure and mining policy

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and environmental loss
frictionVectors.details: Informal and illegal gold mining damages waterways and agricultural land, while enforcement is complicated by local political and economic interests.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is seeking more domestic processing and value capture from bauxite, manganese, and lithium, but financing needs and foreign technical control limit policy flexibility.

highlights: Simandou is reshaping Guinea's strategic bargaining power
Junta nationalism collides with heavy foreign project dependence

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor control
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore project depends on foreign-led mine, rail, and port investment, creating major opportunities for state revenue but also long-term exposure to Chinese and multinational leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Transition and contract uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: The military government uses resource nationalism to strengthen its position, while uncertainty over elections, licenses, and investor terms raises political and operational risk.

highlights: Cashew exports remain the economy's strategic bottleneck
Political fragility weakens control of ports and maritime resources

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country exports most cashew with limited processing, leaving farmers and state revenues exposed to foreign traders, price swings, and external market concentration.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime and port influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and external commercial interests compete for access to coastal resources, while weak institutions limit effective maritime monitoring and port governance.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked reforms and substantial Chinese and private infrastructure exposure constrain Nairobi's fiscal room. Debt servicing remains a sovereignty concern even as Kenya diversifies its financing partners.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Lamu port and transport corridors are strategically contested by regional and external commercial interests. Emerging critical-mineral projects could reproduce enclave extraction unless local processing and revenue safeguards improve.

frictionVectors.title: South African Water Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports to South Africa provide essential revenue but leave the kingdom dependent on Pretoria for infrastructure, payments, and downstream access. The arrangement limits independent control over its most valuable strategic resource.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Owned Industrial Base
frictionVectors.details: The garment sector remains vulnerable to foreign demand, preferential trade access, and external ownership. Any loss of market access can rapidly weaken employment and fiscal stability.

frictionVectors.title: Concessionary Mining Model
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, gold, and prospective mineral projects are dominated by foreign capital and concession structures that can limit domestic value capture. Weak enforcement capacity increases the risk of revenue leakage and community conflict.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia's port and major transport corridors depend heavily on external operators, lenders, and development partners. This improves connectivity but leaves infrastructure policy exposed to competing foreign commercial interests.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Revenue Contest
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security networks continue to compete over the National Oil Corporation, export terminals, and revenue allocation. Production remains vulnerable to blockades, militia pressure, and disputes between eastern and western authorities.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Patronage
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked forces, Egypt, the UAE, and other actors retain influence through military, political, or economic channels. Their presence entrenches fragmented security arrangements and limits unified Libyan control of territory and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dominance
frictionVectors.details: Large nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mining operations rely on foreign capital, technology, and export markets. Fiscal gains are significant but remain vulnerable to contract disputes, commodity prices, and weak domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Power shortages, ports, and transport corridors depend heavily on external lenders and investors. These gaps increase bargaining power for foreign mining and infrastructure partners while constraining Madagascar's policy autonomy.

highlights: Energy and Fertilizer Dependence Remain Acute

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed reforms and creditor negotiations constrain fiscal policy and public investment. Dependence on external budget support limits Malawi's room to direct strategic infrastructure on its own terms.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Power Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Foreign participation is increasingly important in uranium and other mineral projects, while unreliable electricity limits domestic processing and value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Contract Confrontations
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is using revised mining terms and regulatory pressure to demand a larger state share from foreign operators. Disputes risk production interruptions, arbitration, and reduced investor confidence.

frictionVectors.title: Security Dependence on Russia
frictionVectors.details: Russian military support expands the junta's strategic autonomy from France and Western partners, but creates dependence on an external security provider and raises concerns over opaque resource-linked arrangements.

highlights: Iron and Fisheries Remain Externally Exposed

frictionVectors.title: Greater Tortue Ahmeyim Sovereignty Test
frictionVectors.details: Offshore gas development with Senegal and international operators offers major revenue potential but leaves Mauritania reliant on foreign technology, finance, and export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Resource Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, ports, fisheries, and planned green-hydrogen projects remain tied to foreign capital and logistics partners. Weak domestic processing limits the share of value retained locally.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and Diego Garcia Negotiations
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius is pressing its sovereignty claim while balancing the strategic interests of the United Kingdom and United States around Diego Garcia. Any settlement must reconcile legal ownership, security access, and regional diplomatic credibility.

frictionVectors.title: External Trade and Finance Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains highly dependent on global tourism, financial services, and preferential market access. Regulatory pressure from larger financial centers can constrain domestic policy autonomy.

highlights: Western Sahara Remains the Strategic Fault Line

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco uses phosphate, fisheries, ports, and renewable-energy development in Western Sahara to reinforce its sovereignty claim. The strategy continues to generate opposition from Algeria, the Polisario Front, and some international legal and political actors.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure Partnerships and Dependency
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf, Chinese, and other external investors are central to ports, rail, energy, and industrial expansion. Rabat retains strong state direction, but financing and technology partnerships create strategic exposure.

highlights: Rwanda-backed stabilization continues in Cabo Delgado

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado LNG Security
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-led gas projects remain dependent on external security support and uncertain conditions around insurgent activity. This limits Maputo's practical control over the timing and terms of resource monetization.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Ports, railways, energy projects, and LNG logistics rely heavily on foreign capital and operators, creating leverage for Gulf, Chinese, and Western partners.

highlights: Oil and green hydrogen raise bargaining power
Walvis Bay becomes a regional energy gateway

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Ownership and Local Benefits
frictionVectors.details: New offshore oil discoveries could strengthen state revenues, but major international operators retain the capital and technical leverage. Local-content expectations will test the government's negotiating position.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Interest in Walvis Bay and green-hydrogen corridors is expanding Namibia's strategic relevance while increasing competition among Gulf, European, Chinese, and regional investors.

highlights: Oil and uranium remain constrained by insecurity

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Realignment
frictionVectors.details: The junta's break with France and reduced Western security cooperation have increased reliance on Russia-linked support while weakening established counterterrorism partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Export and Pipeline Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The China-backed oil pipeline and southern export route are exposed to political friction, regional isolation, and militant disruption. Niger's landlocked geography limits its leverage over resource revenues.

highlights: Oil governance remains undermined by theft

frictionVectors.title: Niger Delta Production Losses
frictionVectors.details: Oil theft, sabotage, and aging infrastructure continue to reduce state capture of hydrocarbon value. Foreign operators are divesting some assets, shifting operational and financial burdens toward Nigerian institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Capital Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Refining expansion improves sovereignty, but power, rail, ports, and upstream investment still depend on complex foreign financing and technology partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Mineral and Security Nexus
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's regional security posture and mineral-trading networks face sustained international scrutiny over alleged links to armed groups and access to eastern Congolese resources.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Investment Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Kigali retains strong bargaining capacity but remains exposed to donor conditionality, sanctions risk, and dependence on foreign investment for infrastructure and export growth.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea exploration
frictionVectors.details: International firms retain interest in disputed or underexplored offshore blocks, but commercially viable production has yet to materialize. Weak state capacity limits São Tomé and Príncipe's leverage in licensing negotiations.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country relies heavily on foreign financing and technical support for ports, energy, and maritime surveillance. Competition among European, Chinese, and other partners offers options but also increases strategic dependency.

highlights: First oil and gas revenues reshape sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-operated hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: Sangomar oil and Greater Tortue Ahmeyim gas are increasing state revenues, but foreign operators and financing remain central to production. Dakar is seeking stronger domestic participation, contract transparency, and revenue protection.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and coastal infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing access and offshore energy development create recurring tensions with artisanal fishing communities. Port, gas, and maritime projects also raise concerns over environmental safeguards and local economic displacement.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing access
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles depends on foreign fleets and investment for its tuna economy, creating continuing disputes over licensing, value capture, and monitoring. The country is strengthening maritime governance but remains exposed to external market power.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean security partnerships
frictionVectors.details: India, France, the United States, and other partners support maritime surveillance and port connectivity. These relationships improve security while requiring careful balancing to preserve Seychelles' strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and mineral dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore, rutile, and other mining operations provide essential revenue but leave the state exposed to commodity cycles and foreign capital. Contract terms, taxation, environmental impacts, and community benefits remain contentious.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics influence
frictionVectors.details: Mining exports depend on externally financed transport and port infrastructure, giving foreign operators substantial leverage over value chains. Freetown is attempting to improve domestic processing and oversight, but implementation remains uneven.

frictionVectors.title: Oil licensing and Turkish partnership
frictionVectors.details: Somalia is promoting offshore exploration and expanding energy cooperation with Turkey, but licensing and revenue-sharing arrangements remain politically contested. Limited regulatory capacity makes equitable control of future petroleum wealth uncertain.

frictionVectors.title: Ports, maritime security, and foreign bases
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the Gulf states, China, the United States, and European actors compete for influence over ports, security assistance, and maritime routes. External support is vital against piracy and militant threats, yet it can deepen federal-regional rivalries and constrain sovereign decision-making.

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL PARTNERSHIP LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is courting diversified investment in platinum, manganese and rare-earth value chains while resisting excessive dependence on any single external bloc. Disputes over beneficiation, ownership and regulatory uncertainty continue to slow projects.

frictionVectors.title: LOGISTICS AND ENERGY CONSTRAINTS
frictionVectors.details: Grid weakness, port congestion and rail failures reduce sovereign control over export capacity and encourage private or foreign-backed infrastructure solutions. State recovery efforts are constrained by fiscal pressure and governance concerns.

frictionVectors.title: PIPELINE DEPENDENCE THROUGH SUDAN
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil exports depend on infrastructure crossing war-affected Sudan, leaving production and public revenue exposed to blockade, sabotage and bargaining by external authorities. Chinese and regional commercial interests remain important but cannot secure the route alone.

frictionVectors.title: RESOURCE REVENUE AND SECURITY PATRONAGE
frictionVectors.details: Oil proceeds and opaque contracting continue to underpin elite and armed-group networks rather than broad state capacity. Regional mediation and foreign security engagement have limited leverage while domestic power-sharing remains fragile.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD AND EXTERNAL WAR FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and export channels are contested by the armed factions and connected to regional trading and financing networks. This weakens civilian control of mineral revenue and increases foreign leverage over the conflict economy.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND OIL INFRASTRUCTURE DISRUPTION
frictionVectors.details: Fighting threatens transport corridors, refineries and the infrastructure used to move South Sudanese oil through Sudan. Control of Port Sudan and adjacent logistics has become both a military asset and a bargaining tool for outside partners.

highlights: LNG and rail projects deepen external stakes

frictionVectors.title: LNG TERMS AND LOCAL CONTENT
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking stronger fiscal, domestic-processing and local-content provisions in long-delayed offshore LNG development. Negotiations must balance sovereign control against the scale of capital and technical expertise required from foreign energy firms.

frictionVectors.title: CORRIDOR COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed rail and port links, Gulf commercial interest and Western critical-minerals engagement are increasing competition around Tanzania's transport corridors. Dar es Salaam is using this rivalry to diversify partners, but debt, concession and environmental risks remain.

highlights: Lomé consolidates as a regional trade hub

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEPENDENCE AND FOREIGN CAPITAL
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé remains central to Togo's trade and regional influence, but its expansion and logistics ecosystem rely heavily on foreign operators, lenders and shipping networks. Revenue gains are offset by exposure to external commercial and security pressures.

frictionVectors.title: PHOSPHATE VALUE-CHAIN CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate remains a strategic export, yet processing capacity, governance and investment constraints limit domestic value capture. Foreign technology and financing can expand output while leaving the state vulnerable to unfavorable terms and commodity-price swings.

frictionVectors.title: Migration and financial conditionality
frictionVectors.details: European partners tie border-control cooperation and financial support to migration management, giving external actors substantial leverage over Tunisian policy.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on imported hydrocarbons and cross-border electricity limits Tunisia's strategic room while renewable projects attract foreign capital and influence.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP sovereignty dispute
frictionVectors.details: The Lake Albert oil project promises export revenue but leaves Uganda exposed to foreign operators, financing conditions, environmental criticism, and a long pipeline route through Tanzania.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-backed infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other external lenders remain important to transport and energy construction, raising concerns about repayment pressure and limited domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of copper value chains
frictionVectors.details: International firms dominate major mining, processing, and trading channels, while Lusaka seeks greater local processing, tax compliance, and bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Power shortages threaten industrial sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Hydropower shortfalls and drought-driven generation losses increase reliance on regional electricity imports and complicate expansion of domestic copper refining.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and platinum bargaining gap
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors are accelerating access to lithium, platinum, and other strategic minerals, while Zimbabwe struggles to secure transparent contracts, domestic processing, and durable fiscal returns.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and financial isolation
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions and restricted financing push Harare toward selective reliance on China and other non-Western partners, increasing external dependence and reducing investment options.
